analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended; Congress instead passed a broader 2001 tax law (H.R. 1836) that phased down the estate tax.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the estate and gift tax entirely for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2004, and would eliminate the tax on transfers that skip a generation. Only the estates of very wealthy people owe the estate tax, so the money goes almost entirely to heirs of large fortunes. The bill got a sponsor but zero cosponsors and never left committee. The House instead addressed estate taxes in the larger 2001 tax cut law, H.R. 1836.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. Under the tax rules in effect in 2001, only estates above roughly $675,000 (double for married couples) owed any estate tax, so repeal would concentrate its benefits on the families of the wealthiest few percent of decedents, with the largest sums going to the very largest estates. Wealth-management and estate-planning professionals would lose business they otherwise retain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate and gift taxes, with repeal applying to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2004 [S3].
The CRS summary states the bill repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and tax on generation-skipping transfers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raised tens of billions of dollars a year, nearly all from estates above the multi-million-dollar exemption level, so repeal would have to be paid for through borrowing, spending cuts, or higher taxes on everyone else. The bill contains no replacement revenue [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers, via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The repeal is unconditional and applies to every estate above zero after 2004, with no replacement revenue, so the entire cost falls on the general Treasury while the benefit goes to heirs of the largest estates [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the estate tax touches only a small share of families, so the bill delivers nothing to the vast majority of households while removing a major progressive source of federal revenue [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it goes to heirs of estates large enough to owe the tax. The cost is broad: the lost revenue would otherwise fund government services or reduce deficits, and it would be made up by everyone else. On balance this is a large, targeted transfer to the wealthiest families paid for by the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, no cosponsor signed on, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended — its subject was instead taken up in the broader 2001 tax cut bill, H.R. 1836 [S5].

narrative.text: Joe Scarborough introduced the bill on February 28, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
The only further recorded action was an August 13, 2001 entry pointing to H.R. 1836, the broader tax bill Congress was assembling that year; the committee never voted on H.R. 799 itself [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death had little practical effect on the outcome: Congress enacted the 2001 tax law (H.R. 1836) that year, which included phased reductions and scheduled repeal of the estate tax. Heirs of large estates gained through that route regardless.

for.name: Joe Scarborough
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill and it drew no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record; the Republican sponsor's party controlled the House and Ways and Means.

industries.note: Repeal would let the largest estates pass their full value to heirs tax-free after 2004, with the benefit concentrated on the top few percent of estates. The cost is the lost federal revenue, borne by everyone else [S3].
A full repeal would shrink the market for estate tax planning and trust services built around the estate and gift tax. This is a modest effect next to the tax change itself.
